subject: GEOGRAPHY
name: Resources
summary: What turns a thing into a resource, and what happens when it runs out.
source: NCERT Class 8 Geography (Resources and Development), syllabus topic coverage only
licence: Original questions written for EduLink · CC BY-SA 4.0

choices: That it has utility — it can be used to satisfy a human need
That it is found underground
That it can be bought and sold for money
That it exists in large quantities
questions.solution: A resource is anything that can be used to satisfy a need, provided it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable. Utility is the key idea: the same substance can be a resource in one place and useless in another. Quantity has nothing to do with it — air is abundant and a resource, while a rare mineral nobody can use is not.

questions.stem: Which of these is a renewable resource?
choices: Solar energy
Coal
Petroleum
Natural gas
questions.solution: Renewable resources are replenished quickly enough by natural processes to be used indefinitely — solar energy, wind, water and forests among them. Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels formed over millions of years, so on any human timescale they are non-renewable: once burnt, they are not coming back.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an actual resource and a potential resource?
choices: An actual resource has a known quantity and is being used now; a potential resource exists but is not yet used
An actual resource is renewable and a potential resource is non-renewable
An actual resource is man-made and a potential resource is natural
There is no difference; the terms mean the same thing
questions.solution: Actual resources are those whose quantity is known and which are being used, such as the coal currently being mined in Jharkhand. Potential resources exist in a region but are not yet in use — the solar potential of Rajasthan was potential for a long time before the technology and money arrived to develop it. Notice that a potential resource can become actual without any new deposit being found; what changes is technology or economics.

questions.stem: Which of these is a pair of biotic and abiotic resources, in that order?
choices: Forests and rocks
Rocks and minerals
Fish and cattle
Soil and water
questions.solution: Biotic resources come from the living world — plants, animals, forests, fisheries and human beings. Abiotic resources are non-living — rocks, minerals, metals, water and land. Forests are biotic and rocks are abiotic, so that pair is in the right order. Fish and cattle are both biotic, and rocks and minerals are both abiotic, so neither of those pairs shows the contrast.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a ubiquitous resource and a localised resource?
choices: A ubiquitous resource is found everywhere; a localised resource is found only in certain places
A ubiquitous resource is renewable; a localised one is not
A ubiquitous resource is owned by the state; a localised one is privately owned
A ubiquitous resource is biotic; a localised one is abiotic
questions.solution: Ubiquitous resources are available everywhere, such as the air we breathe. Localised resources are concentrated in particular places — copper and iron ore occur only where the geology put them. The distinction matters politically as much as geographically: localised resources create trade, dependence and sometimes conflict, precisely because not everybody has them.

choices: Meeting the needs of the present without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Stopping all use of natural resources immediately
Using resources as quickly as possible to develop faster
Developing only renewable resources and ignoring all others
questions.solution: Sustainable development balances present use against future availability — it does not mean using nothing, which would be neither possible nor desirable. It means using resources at a rate and in a way that leaves the next generation with real choices. The principles that follow from it are practical ones: reduce waste, recycle what can be recycled, and give renewable resources time to replenish.

questions.stem: Why is the conservation of resources necessary even for renewable resources such as forests and groundwater?
choices: Because renewable resources replenish at a limited rate, and using them faster than that rate exhausts them
Because renewable resources are more expensive than non-renewable ones
Because renewable resources cannot be used by more than one country
Because renewable resources become non-renewable after a fixed number of years
questions.solution: Renewable does not mean unlimited — it means replenished by natural processes at some rate. A forest regrows and an aquifer refills, but both do so slowly. If extraction outpaces replenishment, the stock falls year after year regardless of the label, which is exactly what has happened to groundwater in parts of Punjab and Haryana. The useful question is never 'is it renewable?' but 'how fast does it renew, and how fast are we taking it?'

questions.stem: In what sense are people described as a resource?
choices: Because human skill, knowledge and labour are what turn raw materials into anything useful
Because people can be bought and sold
Because population growth always increases a country's wealth
Because people consume resources and so must be counted among them
questions.solution: Nothing in nature is a resource until somebody knows how to use it — so human beings are the resource that creates all the others. Education and health are therefore investments in resources, not merely in welfare, which is why the phrase 'human resource development' exists. Note that it is skill and knowledge that count, not sheer numbers: a large but poorly educated population is not automatically a larger resource.

questions.stem: What is the difference between the 'stock' of a resource and the 'reserve' of a resource?
choices: Stock is the material we lack the technology to use; reserve is the part of the stock we can use now with existing technology
Stock refers to renewable resources and reserve to non-renewable ones
Stock is owned by governments and reserve by private companies
Stock is what is used each year and reserve is what remains
questions.solution: Stock is the portion of the environment with the potential to satisfy a need, but which we cannot yet use for want of technology — hydrogen in water is the standard example, an enormous store of energy we cannot yet tap cheaply. Reserves are the subset that can be drawn on with current technology, like the water in a dam held for generating power. The line between them moves as technology improves, so a stock can become a reserve without anything physical changing.

questions.stem: How far from its coastline does a country's exclusive economic zone extend?
choices: 200 nautical miles
12 nautical miles
50 nautical miles
500 nautical miles
questions.solution: A country's territorial waters extend 12 nautical miles from the coast, but its exclusive economic zone reaches 200 nautical miles. Within that zone the country has exclusive rights to the resources — fish, oil, minerals — though it is not sovereign territory in the way land is, and ships of other nations may pass through. The distinction between the two limits is what the question is really testing.

questions.stem: Petroleum lay in the ground for millions of years before it was considered a resource. What does this best illustrate?
choices: That resources are created by human technology and need, not merely found in nature
That petroleum was not present in the ground before the nineteenth century
That all resources are renewable given enough time
That geology is more important than technology in defining a resource
questions.solution: The petroleum was always there; what changed was that people developed the means to extract it and the engines that made it worth extracting. This is the central argument of the chapter: nature supplies materials, and human beings supply the technology, the need and the economics that turn a material into a resource. It also cuts the other way — a resource can stop being one, as whale oil did once kerosene and electricity replaced it, without a drop of it disappearing.

questions.stem: Why can the same river be a valuable resource for one country and a source of dispute with another?
choices: Because a river crossing a border is used by both, and one country's use upstream changes what reaches the other
Because rivers change their chemical composition when they cross borders
Because international law forbids any country from using a shared river
Because rivers are classified as stock rather than reserve
questions.solution: A river is a localised resource that does not respect borders. Water drawn, dammed or polluted upstream is water that does not arrive downstream in the same quantity or quality, so the two countries' uses are directly in tension. That is why shared rivers are governed by treaties rather than left to ordinary ownership — India and Pakistan's Indus Waters Treaty is the best-known example in this region. The underlying point is that a resource which crosses a boundary cannot be managed by either side alone.
